claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles exhibit preferential Cu enrichment at their surfaces or particle edges.
Cu surface segregation occurs as the nanoparticles approach the premelting regime.
Cu segregates because its intrinsic melting temperature is lower than those of the other constituent metals.
Surface-segregated Cu forms a quasi-liquid Cu-rich layer during premelting.
The quasi-liquid Cu-rich surface layer facilitates subsequent melting into the nanoparticle core.
The as-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are initially homogeneous and have well-mixed elemental distributions.
A suitable dopant or pre-alloying treatment can reduce Cu mobility in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Increasing temperature drives Cu migration from the nanoparticle bulk to its surface.
A Cu-rich surface locally melts at a lower temperature than the remainder of the nanoparticle.
The quasi-liquid Cu layer enhances local diffusion.
The quasi-liquid Cu layer enhances heat transfer and thereby promotes progressive core melting.
Standard FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will develop a quasi-liquid surface layer before bulk melting, observable through TEM contrast changes and reduced local crystallinity.
Nanoparticles engineered to restrict Cu mobility will exhibit delayed or absent surface premelting relative to standard nanoparticles under the same heating conditions.
The relevant premelting and melting behavior is confined to approximately 0.8–1.2 times the melting point of pure Cu.
An inert atmosphere or vacuum minimizes oxidation and extraneous surface reactions during heating.
Failure to detect Cu surface segregation before bulk melting would falsify the proposed segregation-governed melting mechanism.
A lack of difference in surface-melting onset between standard and Cu-mobility-inhibited nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.
